claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2D shows no SUMO1 conjugation to K123/182/592R mutant.

claims.claim: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant fails to translocate into the nucleus.
claims.source: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant lost sumoylation, and failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
claims.evidence: Confocal imaging in Figure 2E shows cytoplasmic localization of K123/182/592R mutant.

claims.claim: IRAK2 sumoylation plays an essential role for IRAK2 nuclear translocation.
claims.source: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant lost sumoylation, and failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that IRAK2 sumoylation plays an essential role for IRAK2 nuclear translocation.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that sumoylation-deficient mutant cannot translocate to the nucleus.

claims.claim: Wild-type IRAK2 is sumoylated in vitro by RanBP2.
claims.source: By in vitro sumoylation assay, we found that wild-type IRAK2 was sumoylated, whereas the K123/182/592R triple mutant failed to be modified (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: In vitro sumoylation assay in Figure 2F shows IRAK2 sumoylation by RanBP2.

claims.claim: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant fails to be sumoylated in vitro.
claims.source: By in vitro sumoylation assay, we found that wild-type IRAK2 was sumoylated, whereas the K123/182/592R triple mutant failed to be modified (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: In vitro sumoylation assay in Figure 2F shows no sumoylation of K123/182/592R mutant.

claims.claim: The modified form of IRAK2 disappears after treatment with SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1.
claims.source: The modified form of IRAK2 disappeared after treatment with SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1, confirming the observed modification of IRAK2 was indeed due to sumoylation (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: Western blot in Figure 2G shows loss of modified IRAK2 band after Ulp1 treatment.

claims.claim: The observed modification of IRAK2 is due to sumoylation.
claims.source: The modified form of IRAK2 disappeared after treatment with SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1, confirming the observed modification of IRAK2 was indeed due to sumoylation (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that Ulp1 treatment removes the modification.

claims.claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation is abolished in the absence of RanBP2.
claims.source: To further assess the importance of RanBP2 in LPS-induced IRAK2 modification, RanBP2 was knocked down in macrophages. LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation was abolished in the absence of RanBP2, confirming that RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2H shows no IRAK2 sumoylation in RanBP2 knockdown cells.

claims.claim: RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation.
claims.source: To further assess the importance of RanBP2 in LPS-induced IRAK2 modification, RanBP2 was knocked down in macrophages. LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation was abolished in the absence of RanBP2, confirming that RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that RanBP2 knockdown abolishes IRAK2 sumoylation.

claims.claim: The sumoylated form of IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBP2.
claims.source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiment showed that the sumoylated form of IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows preferential binding of sumoylated IRAK2 to RanBP2.

claims.claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation is abolished in RanBP2 knock-down cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation was abolished in RanBP2 knock-down cells, supporting the critical role of IRAK2 sumoylation for its nuclear translocation (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Nuclear fractionation data in Figure 2I shows no nuclear IRAK2 in RanBP2 knockdown cells.

claims.claim: IRAK2 sumoylation plays a critical role for its nuclear translocation.
claims.source: Furthermore, LPS-induced IRAK2 nuclear translocation was abolished in RanBP2 knock-down cells, supporting the critical role of IRAK2 sumoylation for its nuclear translocation (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that blocking sumoylation prevents nuclear translocation.

claims.claim: A group of mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) accumulate in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2.
claims.source: We identified a group of mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2, suggesting that IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Microarray analysis in Figure 3A shows nuclear accumulation of these mRNAs in IRAK2 KO cells.

claims.claim: IRAK2 is required for the exportation of Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2 mRNAs.
claims.source: We identified a group of mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2, suggesting that IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that these mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus without IRAK2.

claims.claim: Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2 mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus of IRAK2 kinase inactive macrophages.
claims.source: The same mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) were also accumulated in the nucleus of IRAK2 kinase inactive macrophages, suggesting that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 3B shows nuclear accumulation of these mRNAs in IRAK2 kinase-inactive macrophages.

claims.claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for the exportation of Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2 mRNAs.
claims.source: The same mRNAs (including Cxcl1, Tnf and Cxcl2) were also accumulated in the nucleus of IRAK2 kinase inactive macrophages, suggesting that the kinase activity of IRAK2 is required for the exportation of these mRNAs (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that these mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus in kinase-inactive macrophages.

claims.claim: SRSF1 binding sites are significantly enriched in the 3'UTRs of LPS-induced mRNAs that accumulate in the nucleus of IRAK2-deficient macrophages.
claims.source: As a result, we found that the binding sites of SRSF1 (KGRWGSM, K: G/U; R:G/A; W:A/U; S:G/C; M:A/C) are significantly enriched in the 3'UTRs of the positive set (LPS-induced mRNAs that were accumulated in the nucleus of IRAK2-deficient macrophages compared to that in wild-type macrophages) versus the negative set (LPS-induced mRNAs whose cytosol/nuclear distribution in the macrophages was not affected by IRAK2 deficiency), and this motif significantly improves the fitting to the data than ones based on the background distribution (Likelihood ratio test p-value<0.0004) (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: RNA-READ motif scanner analysis in Figure 3C shows significant enrichment of SRSF1 binding sites.

claims.claim: SRSF1 interacts with IRAK2 in the nucleus.
claims.source: Interestingly, we detected SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction in the nucleus by duo-link assay (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
claims.evidence: Proximity ligation assay in Figure 3D shows SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction in the nucleus.

claims.claim: SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction is abolished for IRAK2 kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.
claims.source: Interestingly, we detected SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction in the nucleus by duo-link assay (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which was abolished for IRAK2 kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.
claims.evidence: Proximity ligation assay in Figure 3D shows no SRSF1-IRAK2 interaction for kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.

claims.claim: IRAK2 can phosphorylate SRSF1 in vitro.
claims.source: Furthermore, IRAK2 was able to phosphorylate SRSF1 in the in vitro kinase assay (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: In vitro kinase assay in Figure 3E shows IRAK2 phosphorylates SRSF1.

claims.claim: LPS induces SRSF1 serine/threonine phosphorylation.
claims.source: In support of this, we found that LPS indeed induced SRSF1 serine/threonine phosphorylation, which was diminished in IRAK2-kinase-inactive nucleus (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3F shows LPS-induced SRSF1 phosphorylation.

claims.claim: LPS-induced SRSF1 phosphorylation is diminished in IRAK2-kinase-inactive nucleus.
claims.source: In support of this, we found that LPS indeed induced SRSF1 serine/threonine phosphorylation, which was diminished in IRAK2-kinase-inactive nucleus (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3F shows reduced SRSF1 phosphorylation in IRAK2 kinase-inactive cells.

claims.claim: SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form (Sanford et al., 2005; Xiao and Manley, 1997)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claims.claim: IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 phosphorylation drives the dissociation of SRSF1 from mRNA targets, promoting their nuclear export.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form (Sanford et al., 2005; Xiao and Manley, 1997), suggesting that IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 phosphorylation probably drives the dissociation of SRSF1 from the mRNA targets, promoting their nuclear export.
claims.evidence: The mechanism is inferred from known SRSF1 behavior and observed IRAK2-mediated phosphorylation.

claims.claim: SRSF1-bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts are increased in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages compared to wild-type cells.
claims.source: By RNA immunoprecipitation, we indeed found that SRSF1-bound transcripts (Cxcl1 and Tnf) were increased in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages compared to that in wild-type cells (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3G shows increased SRSF1 binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf in IRAK2-deficient and kinase-inactive cells.

claims.claim: IRAK2 directly phosphorylates SRSF1 in the nucleus in response to LPS stimulation, facilitating dissociation of SRSF1 from LPS-induced transcripts and their nuclear export.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that IRAK2 may directly phosphorylate SRSF1 in the nucleus in response to LPS stimulation, which facilitates the dissociation of SRSF1 from the LPS-induced transcripts, and the subsequent nuclear export of these mRNAs.
claims.evidence: The mechanism is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing IRAK2-SRSF1 interaction, phosphorylation, and effects on mRNA export.

claims.claim: SRSF1-bound Ctnnb1 transcript is not affected by LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency.
claims.source: Notably, SRSF1 also plays a critical role in regulating genes that are constitutively expressed, such as Ctnnb1 (β-catenin) (Fu et al., 2013). Interestingly, SRSF1-bound transcript Ctnnb1 was not affected by either LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency (Figure 3G), indicating that IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3G shows no change in SRSF1 binding to Ctnnb1 with LPS or IRAK2 deficiency.

claims.claim: IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
claims.source: Notably, SRSF1 also plays a critical role in regulating genes that are constitutively expressed, such as Ctnnb1 (β-catenin) (Fu et al., 2013). Interestingly, SRSF1-bound transcript Ctnnb1 was not affected by either LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency (Figure 3G), indicating that IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that not all SRSF1-bound transcripts are affected by IRAK2.

claims.claim: ALYREF was identified as an IRAK2-interacting protein by mass spectrometry analysis.
claims.source: Importantly, ALYREF nuclear export factor was actually among the proteins based on MS analysis of IRAK2 immunoprecipitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Mass spectrometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 identified ALYREF as an IRAK2-interacting protein.

claims.claim: LPS stimulation induces the interaction of IRAK2 with ALYREF in the nucleus.
claims.source: By coimmunoprecipitation, we found that LPS stimulation induced the interaction of IRAK2 with ALYREF in the nucleus (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows LPS-induced IRAK2-ALYREF interaction in the nucleus.

claims.claim: ALYREF interacts with wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants.
claims.source: Duo-link assay showed that ALYREF interacts with wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Proximity ligation assay in Figure 4B shows ALYREF interaction only with wild-type IRAK2.

claims.claim: IRAK2 kinase activity and sumoylation are required for IRAK2's interaction with ALYREF in the nucleus.
claims.source: Duo-link assay showed that ALYREF interacts with wild-type IRAK2, but not kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1). These results indicate that the kinase activity of IRAK2 and subsequent sumoylation are required for IRAK2's interaction with ALYREF in the nucleus, which is probably due to the fact that the kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants do not interact with ALYREF and do not translocate to the nucleus.

claims.claim: ALYREF is absent in SRSF1 immunoprecipitates.
claims.source: Since LPS-induced the interaction of IRAK2 with SRSF1 (Figures 3D–F and 4A), we wondered whether IRAK2-SRSF1 and IRAK2-ALYREF belong to one complex. Interestingly, ALYREF was absent in the SRSF1 immunoprecipitates, while SRSF1 was also not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows no ALYREF in SRSF1 immunoprecipitates.

claims.claim: SRSF1 is not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates.
claims.source: Since LPS-induced the interaction of IRAK2 with SRSF1 (Figures 3D–F and 4A), we wondered whether IRAK2-SRSF1 and IRAK2-ALYREF belong to one complex. Interestingly, ALYREF was absent in the SRSF1 immunoprecipitates, while SRSF1 was also not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows no SRSF1 in ALYREF immunoprecipitates.

claims.claim: IRAK2 is detected in both SRSF1 and ALYREF immunoprecipitates in response to LPS stimulation.
claims.source: On the other hand, IRAK2 was detected in either SRSF1 or ALYREF immunoprecipitates in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A shows IRAK2 in both SRSF1 and ALYREF immunoprecipitates.

claims.claim: LPS-induced IRAK2's interaction with SRSF1 and ALYREF are mutually exclusive.
claims.source: Interestingly, ALYREF was absent in the SRSF1 immunoprecipitates, while SRSF1 was also not detected in ALYREF immunoprecipitates (Figure 4A). On the other hand, IRAK2 was detected in either SRSF1 or ALYREF immunoprecipitates in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 4A). These results suggest that LPS-induced IRAK2's interaction with SRSF1 and ALYREF are mutually exclusive.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that SRSF1 and ALYREF do not co-immunoprecipitate but both interact with IRAK2.

claims.claim: LPS stimulation induces the binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf mRNAs.
claims.source: In support of this, RIP analysis showed that LPS stimulation induced the binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to the mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf, and ALYREF's binding to the mRNAs was substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figures 4C-D shows LPS-induced binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to these mRNAs.

claims.claim: ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf mRNAs is substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages.
claims.source: In support of this, RIP analysis showed that LPS stimulation induced the binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to the mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf, and ALYREF's binding to the mRNAs was substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and IRAK2-kinase-inactive macrophages (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4D shows reduced ALYREF binding in IRAK2-deficient and kinase-inactive cells.

claims.claim: ALYREF-bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts are increased in SRSF1 knock-down cells, even in IRAK2 KO macrophages.
claims.source: Interestingly, ALYREF bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts were increased in SRSF1 knock-down cells, even in IRAK2 KO macrophages, indicating that ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf is no longer IRAK2-dependent in the absence of SRSF1 (Figure 4E and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E shows increased ALYREF binding in SRSF1 knockdown cells.

claims.claim: ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf is no longer IRAK2-dependent in the absence of SRSF1.
claims.source: Interestingly, ALYREF bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts were increased in SRSF1 knock-down cells, even in IRAK2 KO macrophages, indicating that ALYREF's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf is no longer IRAK2-dependent in the absence of SRSF1 (Figure 4E and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that ALYREF binds target mRNAs in SRSF1 knockdown cells even without IRAK2.

claims.claim: ALYREF-bound Ctnnb1 mRNA is not affected by LPS stimulation, IRAK2 deficiency or SRSF1 knockdown.
claims.source: Similar to SRSF1, ALYREF also binds to constitutively expressed Ctnnb1 mRNA. Importantly, ALYREF-bound Ctnnb1 mRNA was not affected by LPS stimulation, IRAK2 deficiency or SRSF1 knockdown (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E shows no change in ALYREF binding to Ctnnb1 under various conditions.

claims.claim: The role of IRAK2 for ALYREF's binding to target mRNAs is to remove SRSF1 from the targets.
claims.source: These results confirmed that the role of IRAK2 for ALYREF's binding to the target mRNAs is probably to remove SRSF1 from the targets.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that ALYREF can bind target mRNAs without IRAK2 when SRSF1 is absent.

claims.claim: Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA is efficiently exported to the cytosol in SRSF1 knockdown cells in the absence of IRAK2.
claims.source: Consistently, whereas IRAK2 deficiency resulted in nuclear accumulation of Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA, Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA was efficiently exported to the cytosol in SRSF1 knockdown cells in the absence of IRAK2 (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 4F shows cytosolic localization of Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNA in SRSF1 knockdown cells even without IRAK2.

claims.claim: LPS stimulation induces the interaction of IRAK2 with Nxf1.
claims.source: In addition to the LPS-induced interaction of IRAK2 with ALYREF, we found that LPS stimulation also induced the interaction of IRAK2 with Nxf1 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A shows LPS-induced IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction.

claims.claim: IRAK2 fails to interact with Nxf1 in the absence of ALYREF.
claims.source: IRAK2 failed to interact with Nxf1 in the absence of ALYREF, suggesting that IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for ALYREF to facilitate the assembly of nuclear export complex to the target mRNAs, including the recruitment of Nxf1 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A shows no IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction in ALYREF knockdown cells.

claims.claim: IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for ALYREF to facilitate the assembly of nuclear export complex to target mRNAs, including recruitment of Nxf1.
claims.source: IRAK2 failed to interact with Nxf1 in the absence of ALYREF, suggesting that IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for ALYREF to facilitate the assembly of nuclear export complex to the target mRNAs, including the recruitment of Nxf1 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction requires ALYREF.

claims.claim: LPS stimulation induces Nxf1's binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNAs in an ALYREF- and IRAK2-dependent manner.
claims.source: In support of this, LPS stimulation induced Nxf1's binding to the mRNAs in an ALYREF- and IRAK2-dependent manner (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figures 5B-D shows LPS-induced Nxf1 binding that is reduced in ALYREF and IRAK2 knockdown/knockout cells.

claims.claim: LPS-induced Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus in the absence of ALYREF.
claims.source: To further assess the importance of ALYREF in LPS-induced IRAK2-dependent mRNA nuclear export, we measured nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA levels in ALYREF knockdown cells. Consistent with the RIP analysis, we found that LPS-induced mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of ALYREF (Figure 5E)
claims.evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 5E shows nuclear accumulation of these mRNAs in ALYREF knockdown cells.

claims.claim: ALYREF is important for IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of inflammatory mRNAs.
claims.source: To further assess the importance of ALYREF in LPS-induced IRAK2-dependent mRNA nuclear export, we measured nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA levels in ALYREF knockdown cells. Consistent with the RIP analysis, we found that LPS-induced mRNAs of Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Tnf accumulated in the nucleus in the absence of ALYREF (Figure 5E), indicating the importance of this nuclear export factor in IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of the inflammatory mRNAs.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that inflammatory mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus without ALYREF.

claims.claim: LPS-induced secretion of CXCL1 and TNF is dramatically reduced in ALYREF knockdown cells.
claims.source: By enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analysis, we showed that LPS-induced secretion of CXCL1 and TNF was dramatically reduced in ALYREF knockdown cells (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: ELISA data in Figure 5F shows reduced cytokine secretion in ALYREF knockdown cells.

claims.claim: SRSF1 binds to Cxcl1 3'UTR (nt 781–901).
claims.source: Using Cxcl1 3'UTR (nt 781–901, which contains stimulus-sensitive motifs (Datta et al., 2010; Hartupee et al., 2007), we validated the SRSF1 binding to this transcript by RNA electrophoretic mobility shift assay (REMSA) (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: REMSA data in Figure 6A shows SRSF1 binding to Cxcl1 3'UTR.

claims.claim: Nucleotides 800–855 in Cxcl1 3'UTR are important for SRSF1 binding.
claims.source: We identified several putative SRSF1-binding motifs in this region of Cxcl1 3'UTR. Deletion analysis and REMSA showed the importance of nt 800–855 in Cxcl1 3'UTR for SRSF1 binding.
claims.evidence: Deletion analysis and REMSA demonstrate the importance of this region for SRSF1 binding.

claims.claim: SRSF1 binds to luciferase reporter mRNA containing the 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940).
claims.source: While SRSF1 RIP precipitated the luciferase reporter mRNA containing the 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), IRAK2 expression reduced SRSF1 binding to the target mRNA (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows SRSF1 binding to luciferase reporter with Cxcl1 3'UTR.

claims.claim: IRAK2 expression reduces SRSF1 binding to luciferase reporter mRNA containing Cxcl1 3'UTR.
claims.source: While SRSF1 RIP precipitated the luciferase reporter mRNA containing the 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), IRAK2 expression reduced SRSF1 binding to the target mRNA (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows reduced SRSF1 binding with IRAK2 expression.

claims.claim: SRSF1 fails to bind luciferase mRNAs with mutated Cxcl1 3'UTR (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835).
claims.source: However, SRSF1 RIP failed to precipitate the luciferase mRNAs with the mutated 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows no SRSF1 binding to mutated constructs.

claims.claim: IRAK2 strongly promotes luciferase activity from constructs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR (721–940).
claims.source: For the cells transfected with wild-type Cxcl1 luciferase construct (with wild-type 3' UTR of Cxcl1 721–940), IRAK2 strongly promoted the luciferase activity (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6C shows increased luciferase activity with IRAK2 expression.

claims.claim: Cytosolic luciferase reporter mRNAs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR are increased in IRAK2-transfected cells.
claims.source: Consistently, the cytosolic luciferase reporter mRNAs (with wild-type 3' UTR of Cxcl1 721–940) were increased in the IRAK2-transfected cells compared to the cells without IRAK2 (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 6D shows increased cytosolic luciferase mRNA with IRAK2.

claims.claim: IRAK2 has reduced ability to promote luciferase activity in cells transfected with mutant Cxcl1 luciferase constructs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835).
claims.source: IRAK2 had much reduced ability to promote luciferase activity in cells transfected with mutant Cxcl1 luciferase constructs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6C shows reduced luciferase activity with mutant constructs.

claims.claim: Removal of the functional SRSF1-binding site traps luciferase reporter mRNAs in the nucleus.
claims.source: Removal of the functional SRSF1-binding site trapped the luciferase reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) in the nucleus and IRAK2 can no longer promote nuclear export of these mutant reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 6D shows nuclear retention of mutant luciferase mRNAs.

claims.claim: IRAK2 cannot promote nuclear export of luciferase reporter mRNAs lacking functional SRSF1-binding sites.
claims.source: Removal of the functional SRSF1-binding site trapped the luciferase reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) in the nucleus and IRAK2 can no longer promote nuclear export of these mutant reporter mRNAs (Cxcl1Δ790–840 and Cxcl1Δ829–835) (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Figure 6D shows IRAK2 cannot promote export of mutant mRNAs.

claims.claim: SRSF1-binding sequence is required for nuclear export promoted by IRAK2.
claims.source: These results suggest that while SRSF1 binding may sequester the luciferase reporter mRNAs in the nucleus, the SRSF1-binding sequence is actually required for nuclear export promoted by IRAK2.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that IRAK2 cannot promote export of mRNAs lacking SRSF1-binding sites.

claims.claim: LPS stimulation induces luciferase activity from cells transfected with constructs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940).
claims.source: LPS stimulation induced luciferase activity from the cells transfected with constructs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), which was abolished in IRAK2-deficient macrophages (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6E shows LPS-induced luciferase activity with wild-type construct.

claims.claim: LPS-induced luciferase activity from constructs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR is abolished in IRAK2-deficient macrophages.
claims.source: LPS stimulation induced luciferase activity from the cells transfected with constructs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940), which was abolished in IRAK2-deficient macrophages (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6E shows no LPS-induced luciferase activity in IRAK2 KO cells.

claims.claim: LPS-induced luciferase activity is substantially reduced in wild-type, IRAK2-deficient or IRAK2-kinase inactive macrophages transfected with mutant luciferase constructs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835).
claims.source: However, LPS-induced luciferase activity was substantially reduced in wild-type, IRAK2-deficient or IRAK2-kinase inactive macrophages transfected with mutant luciferase constructs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 6E shows reduced luciferase activity with mutant constructs in all cell types.

claims.claim: IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of target mRNAs is dependent on SRSF1-binding sites in the target mRNA.
claims.source: These results confirm that IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of the target mRNAs is dependent on the SRSF1-binding sites in the target mRNA.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from luciferase assay results showing that mutant constructs lacking SRSF1-binding sites are not exported by IRAK2.

claims.claim: IRAK2 promotes ALYREF binding to wild-type luciferase reporter mRNAs containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 (nt 721–940).
claims.source: Consistent with the fact that IRAK2 is required for LPS-induced ALYREF's binding to the target mRNAs, IRAK2 promoted ALYREF RIP of wild-type luciferase reporter mRNAs (containing wild-type 3'UTR of Cxcl1 nt 721–940) (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6F shows increased ALYREF binding with IRAK2 expression.

claims.claim: ALYREF reduces binding to mutant luciferase reporter mRNAs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) even in the presence of IRAK2.
claims.source: Interestingly, ALYREF reduced the binding to the mutant luciferase reporter mRNAs (Δ790–840 and Δ829–835) even in the presence of IRAK2 (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6F shows reduced ALYREF binding to mutant constructs.

claims.claim: The SRSF1-binding site is required for ALYREF's binding to target mRNAs.
claims.source: These results suggest that the SRSF1-binding site seems to be required for ALYREF's binding to the target mRNAs.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that ALYREF binding is reduced when SRSF1-binding sites are deleted.

claims.claim: ALYREF can directly bind to the probe containing the SRSF1-binding site (Cxcl1 nt 800–855) in vitro.
claims.source: In support of this, ALYREF can directly bind to the probe that contains the SRSF1-binding site in the in vitro RNA-binding assay (Cxcl1 nt 800–855, Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: REMSA data in Figure 6G shows ALYREF binding to the SRSF1-binding site probe.

claims.claim: The SRSF1-binding site renders LPS-IRAK2 sensitivity of target mRNA for nuclear export via IRAK2-mediated removal of SRSF1 and recruitment of ALYREF.
claims.source: Taken together, our results implicate that the SRSF1-binding site renders the LPS-IRAK2 sensitivity of the target mRNA for the nuclear export possibly via the IRAK2-mediated removal of SRSF1 and recruitment of nuclear export factors ALYREF to the target mRNAs.
claims.evidence: The mechanism is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing the importance of SRSF1-binding sites for IRAK2-mediated export.

claims.claim: IRAK2 kinase-inactive knock-in mice show substantially increased survival after LPS-induced septic shock compared to wild-type mice.
claims.source: We found that IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice showed substantially increased survival after LPS-induced septic shock compared to that of the wild-type mice (Figure 7A)(Mao et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Survival curve data in Figure 7A shows increased survival in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.

claims.claim: LPS-induced serum CXCL1 and TNF levels are much reduced in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice compared to wild-type mice.
claims.source: Likewise, LPS-induced serum CXCL1 and TNF levels were much reduced in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice compared to that of the wild-type mice (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: ELISA data in Figure 7B shows reduced serum cytokine levels in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.

claims.claim: LPS/TLR4 engagement activates a nuclear function of IRAK2 that facilitates assembly of nuclear export machinery to export inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for protein translation.
claims.source: In this study, we report that LPS/TLR4 engagement activates a nuclear function of IRAK2 that facilitates the assembly of nuclear export machinery to enable export the inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for protein translation.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for RanBP2-mediated IRAK2 sumoylation and nuclear translocation.
claims.source: IRAK2 kinase activity is required for RanBP2-mediated IRAK2 sumoylation and nuclear translocation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing that kinase-inactive mutants are not sumoylated and do not translocate to the nucleus.

claims.claim: Nuclear IRAK2 phosphorylates SRSF1 and reduces SRSF1 binding to target mRNAs.
claims.source: Nuclear IRAK2 then phosphorylates SRSF1 and reduces SRSF1 binding to the target mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from in vitro kinase assays and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: LPS induces interaction between IRAK2 and nuclear export adaptor ALYREF to replace SRSF1 on target mRNAs.
claims.source: At the same time, LPS induces interaction between IRAK2 and nuclear export adaptor ALYREF to replace SRSF1 on the target mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: Recruited ALYREF bridges the interaction between mRNA targets and nuclear export receptor Nxf1, triggering Nxf1 loading for mRNA export.
claims.source: The recruited ALYREF in turn bridges the interaction between the mRNA targets and nuclear export receptor Nxf1, triggering nuclear export receptor Nxf1 loading for the export of the mRNAs. (Figure 7C)
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments showing ALYREF-dependent Nxf1 recruitment.

claims.claim: LPS-induced IRAK2 activation provides a critical check point for production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines by controlling nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution of LPS-induced transcripts.
claims.source: Therefore, LPS-induced IRAK2 activation provides a critical check point for the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines by controlling the nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution of the LPS-induced transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings in the study.

claims.claim: Atypical kinases such as KSR2 and CASK have been reported to carry catalytic activity.
claims.source: Notably, atypical kinases such as KSR2 (Brennan et al., 2011) and CASK (Mukherjee et al., 2008) have been reported to carry catalytic activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claims.claim: Mutations in the ATP-binding site and catalytic residues impaired the function of IRAK2.
claims.source: We found recombinant IRAK2 was able to autophophorylate and phosphorylate MBP and SRSF1; mutations in the ATP-binding site and catalytic residues impaired the function of IRAK2.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from in vitro kinase assays and functional studies.

claims.claim: IRAK2 kinase activity is critical for the function of IRAK2 in LPS-induced pro-inflammatory response.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that the IRAK2 kinase activity is critical for the function of IRAK2 in LPS-induced pro-inflammatory response.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing that kinase-inactive IRAK2 cannot restore inflammatory responses.

claims.claim: RanBP2 is a major nucleoporin that extends cytoplasmic filaments from the nuclear pore complex and contains phenylalanine–glycine repeats that bind nuclear transport receptors of the importin beta family.
claims.source: While importin-β is one of the transport receptor mediating translocation of molecules into the cell nucleus, RanBP2 is a major nucleoporin that extends cytoplasmic filaments from the nuclear pore complex and contains phenylalanine–glycine repeats that bind nuclear transport receptors of the importin beta family (Wu et al., 1995; Yokoyama et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of IRAK2 at S136 and T140 affects its interaction with RanBP2.
claims.source: Our data showed that mutations in putative IRAK2 phosphorylation sites S136/T140 (Weintz et al., 2010) substantially reduced the interaction of IRAK2 with RanBP2.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation experiments with phosphorylation site mutants.

claims.claim: ALYREF and SRSF1 belong to the same family of proteins called the shuttling SR (serine- and arginine-rich) proteins, sharing a similar RNA-binding domain.
claims.source: Notably, ALYREF and SRSF1 actually belong to the same family of proteins called the shuttling SR (serine- and arginine-rich) proteins, sharing a similar RNA-binding domain.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these proteins.

claims.claim: SRSF1 and ALYREF can bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif.
claims.source: Indeed, we found SRSF1 and ALYREF were able to bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from REMSA experiments showing both proteins bind the same motif.

claims.claim: Removal of SRSF1 allows nuclear export adaptor ALYREF binding to target mRNAs.
claims.source: Indeed, we found SRSF1 and ALYREF were able to bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif; and the removal of SRSF1 allowed nuclear export adaptor ALYREF binding to the target mRNAs
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from RNA immunoprecipitation experiments in SRSF1 knockdown cells.

claims.claim: SRSF1-mediated nuclear sequestration of target mRNAs is achieved by blocking the binding of ALYREF to the mRNAs.
claims.source: Indeed, we found SRSF1 and ALYREF were able to bind to the same SRSF1-binding motif; and the removal of SRSF1 allowed nuclear export adaptor ALYREF binding to the target mRNAs, suggesting that SRSF1-mediated nuclear sequestration of target mRNAs might be achieved by blocking the binding of ALYREF to the mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This mechanism is inferred from the observation that SRSF1 and ALYREF bind the same motif and SRSF1 removal allows ALYREF binding.

claims.claim: ALYREF (a subunit of the TREX complex) makes contact with nuclear export receptor Nxf1, serving as a bridge between mRNA and Nxf1.
claims.source: Importantly, previous studies have reported that ALYREF (a subunit of the so-called TREX complex for nuclear export) makes contact with nuclear export receptor Nxf1, serving as a bridge between mRNA and nuclear export receptor Nxf1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on previous studies about ALYREF function.

claims.claim: Nuclear IRAK2 mediates removal of SRSF1 and facilitates assembly of nuclear export machinery to export inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for translation.
claims.source: Thus, nuclear IRAK2 mediates the removal of SRSF1 and facilitates the assembly of nuclear export machinery to export the inflammatory mRNAs to the cytosol for translation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: About 10–30% of LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts are exported out of the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2.
claims.source: Interestingly, about 10–30% LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts were exported out of the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2 (Figure 3B)
claims.evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 3B shows partial export of inflammatory transcripts in IRAK2 KO cells.

claims.claim: There might be another mechanism besides IRAK2 that allows ALYREF binding to target mRNAs for nuclear export.
claims.source: Interestingly, about 10–30% LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts were exported out of the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2 (Figure 3B), which was consistent with the residual ALYREF's binding to these transcripts in IRAK2-/- cells (Figure 4D). These results implicate that there might be yet another mechanism besides IRAK2 that allows ALYREF binding to the target mRNAs for nuclear export.
claims.evidence: This possibility is inferred from the observation that some export occurs without IRAK2.

results.result: IRAK2 is an atypical kinase with amino acid substitutions in key catalytic residues (Asp->Asn333; Asp->His351), yet recombinant wild-type IRAK2 demonstrates kinase activity by autophosphorylating and phosphorylating MBP, while kinase-inactive mutants (KK235AA, H351A) show minimal activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are directly supported by structural modeling (Figure 1A) and in vitro kinase assays (Figure 1B). The comparison to other atypical kinases (C119) provides appropriate context. The data clearly demonstrate that despite atypical residues, IRAK2 possesses measurable kinase activity that is abolished by mutations in the ATP-binding site and catalytic residues.

results.result: IRAK2 kinase activity is necessary for LPS-induced inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production, as demonstrated by rescue experiments in IRAK2-deficient macrophages and reduced cytokine production in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 are well-supported by complementary approaches: reconstitution experiments in IRAK2-deficient cells (Figure 1C, E) and analysis of kinase-inactive knockin mice (Figure 1D, F). Both ELISA and Western blot data converge on the conclusion that kinase activity is essential for IRAK2 function in inflammatory responses.

results.result: IRAK2 undergoes ligand-dependent modification and nuclear translocation in response to LPS and other TLR ligands (ox-LDL, R848, CpGB), with only wild-type but not kinase-inactive IRAK2 showing this modification and nuclear localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C12-C13 are supported by Western blot analysis showing modified IRAK2 bands (Figure 1E, F) and nuclear fractionation demonstrating nuclear translocation (Figure 1F). The observation extends to multiple TLR ligands (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The requirement for kinase activity is demonstrated in both mutant reconstitution and knockin mice.

results.result: IRAK2 kinase activity is important for nuclear translocation, as kinase-inactive mutants (KK235AA, H351A, N333A) fail to translocate to the nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are supported by confocal imaging (Figure 1G) showing cytoplasmic retention of kinase-inactive mutants. This is consistent with the nuclear fractionation data from kinase-inactive knockin mice (Figure 1F). The inference that kinase activity is important for nuclear translocation is reasonable given the consistent phenotype across multiple mutants.

results.result: IRAK2 contains a putative NLS (Aa 357-366: HPDNKKTKYT) that is required for nuclear translocation and IRAK2-mediated inflammatory gene expression, with the NLS mutant failing to translocate, restore cytokine production, or undergo modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 are supported by confocal imaging showing cytoplasmic retention of NLS mutant (Figure 1G), failure to restore cytokine production (Figure 1C), and lack of modification (Figure 1E). The identification of the NLS is based on sequence analysis, and the functional importance is demonstrated through mutagenesis. The link between nuclear translocation and modification (C19) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: IRAK2 interacts with importin-β and RanBP2, with kinase-inactive mutants retaining importin-β binding but losing RanBP2 interaction, while the NLS mutant fails to bind importin-β, indicating that kinase activity is not required for NLS-importin engagement but is required for RanBP2 interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are supported by mass spectrometry identification (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2A). The differential binding patterns of various mutants provide clear evidence for the distinct requirements for importin-β versus RanBP2 interaction. The conclusion about kinase activity requirements (C24) is well-supported by the mutant analysis.

results.result: LPS-induced phosphorylation of IRAK2 at S136 and T140 is required for RanBP2 interaction and nuclear localization, with the S136A/T140A double mutant abolishing both while retaining importin-β binding, suggesting IRAK2 auto-phosphorylation at these sites mediates RanBP2 interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by prior literature (C26, cited from Weintz et al., 2010) and experimental data showing loss of RanBP2 binding and nuclear localization in the S136A/T140A mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) while importin-β binding is retained. The inference about auto-phosphorylation (C30) is reasonable given the kinase activity of IRAK2 and the requirement for these sites.

results.result: The modified, phosphorylated form of IRAK2 preferentially binds to RanBP2.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation showing preferential binding of modified IRAK2 to RanBP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and phos-tag gel analysis confirming phosphorylated IRAK2 binds RanBP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). These complementary approaches provide strong evidence for the preferential interaction.

results.result: RanBP2 carries an active SUMO E3 ligase domain and IRAK2 has been characterized as a sumoylated protein in proteomics studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by citations to prior literature (Pichler et al., 2002 for C33; Lamoliatte et al., 2014 for C34). These establish the relevant background knowledge for the subsequent experiments on IRAK2 sumoylation.

results.result: LPS stimulation induces IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction and IRAK2 sumoylation by SUMO1, both of which are abolished in IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice, confirming that IRAK2 kinase activity is required for RanBP2 interaction and sumoylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing LPS-induced IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction (Figure 2B) and SUMO1 conjugation under denaturing conditions (Figure 2C), both abolished in kinase-inactive knockin mice. The use of denaturing conditions for sumoylation detection is appropriate to distinguish direct conjugation from complex formation.

results.result: IRAK2 K123/182/592R triple mutant loses sumoylation and fails to translocate to the nucleus, indicating that IRAK2 sumoylation plays an essential role in nuclear translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation showing loss of sumoylation (Figure 2D) and confocal imaging showing cytoplasmic retention (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) of the K123/182/592R mutant. The inference that sumoylation is essential for nuclear translocation (C42) is well-supported by the consistent phenotype.

results.result: Wild-type IRAK2 is sumoylated in vitro by RanBP2 while the K123/182/592R mutant is not, and the modified form of IRAK2 is sensitive to SUMO-specific isopeptidase Ulp1, confirming the modification is sumoylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by in vitro sumoylation assays (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5) and Ulp1 treatment experiments (Figure 2G). The use of purified recombinant proteins and SUMO-specific protease provides strong biochemical evidence that the modification is indeed sumoylation.

results.result: RanBP2 is the E3 ligase for IRAK2 sumoylation, as demonstrated by loss of LPS-induced IRAK2 sumoylation and nuclear translocation in RanBP2 knockdown cells, with sumoylated IRAK2 preferentially binding RanBP2.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by RanBP2 knockdown experiments showing loss of IRAK2 sumoylation (Figure 2H) and nuclear translocation (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), along with co-immunoprecipitation showing preferential binding of sumoylated IRAK2 to RanBP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). The conclusion that RanBP2 is the E3 ligase (C48) is well-supported by the knockdown data.

results.result: A group of mRNAs (Cxcl1, Tnf, Cxcl2) accumulate in the nucleus in the absence of IRAK2 or in IRAK2 kinase-inactive macrophages, indicating that IRAK2 kinase activity is required for exportation of these mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by microarray analysis (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and RT-PCR (Figure 3B) showing nuclear accumulation of specific mRNAs in IRAK2 KO and kinase-inactive cells. The inference that IRAK2 is required for export (C54, C56) is reasonable given the nuclear accumulation phenotype.

results.result: SRSF1 binding sites are significantly enriched in the 3'UTRs of LPS-induced mRNAs that accumulate in the nucleus of IRAK2-deficient macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by RNA-READ motif scanner analysis (Figure 3C) showing significant enrichment (p<0.0004) of SRSF1 binding motifs in the positive set versus negative set. The statistical analysis appears appropriate for identifying enriched motifs, though the manuscript could benefit from more details on the background model and multiple testing correction.

results.result: SRSF1 interacts with IRAK2 in the nucleus (abolished in kinase-inactive and sumoylation mutants), IRAK2 phosphorylates SRSF1 in vitro, and LPS induces SRSF1 phosphorylation that is diminished in IRAK2 kinase-inactive cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by proximity ligation assay (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), in vitro kinase assay (Figure 3E), and co-immunoprecipitation showing SRSF1 phosphorylation (Figure 3F). The convergence of multiple approaches provides strong evidence for IRAK2-SRSF1 interaction and IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 phosphorylation.

results.result: SRSF1 binds RNA in its hypo-phosphorylated form, suggesting IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 phosphorylation drives dissociation from mRNA targets and promotes nuclear export.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by prior literature (Sanford et al., 2005; Xiao and Manley, 1997). Claim C64 is a reasonable mechanistic inference based on established SRSF1 biology and the observed IRAK2-mediated phosphorylation, though direct evidence for dissociation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: SRSF1-bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts are increased in IRAK2-deficient and kinase-inactive macrophages, suggesting IRAK2 directly phosphorylates SRSF1 in the nucleus to facilitate dissociation from LPS-induced transcripts and their nuclear export.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4). Claim C66 is a reasonable synthesis of multiple observations (IRAK2-SRSF1 interaction, phosphorylation, increased SRSF1 binding in IRAK2-deficient cells, and nuclear accumulation of mRNAs), though the mechanism remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: SRSF1-bound Ctnnb1 transcript is not affected by LPS stimulation or IRAK2 deficiency, indicating IRAK2 may only regulate a specific subset of SRSF1-targeted mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by RNA immunoprecipitation showing no change in SRSF1 binding to Ctnnb1 (Figure 3G). This negative control is important for demonstrating specificity of the IRAK2-SRSF1 pathway and strengthens the overall conclusions.

results.result: ALYREF was identified as an IRAK2-interacting protein, with LPS inducing nuclear IRAK2-ALYREF interaction that requires IRAK2 kinase activity and sumoylation (likely due to nuclear translocation requirements).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 are supported by mass spectrometry identification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 4A), and proximity ligation assay (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The inference that kinase activity and sumoylation requirements reflect nuclear translocation requirements (C72) is reasonable given prior data.

results.result: ALYREF and SRSF1 do not co-immunoprecipitate with each other, but both interact with IRAK2 in response to LPS, suggesting LPS-induced IRAK2 interactions with SRSF1 and ALYREF are mutually exclusive.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4A) showing absence of ALYREF in SRSF1 IPs and vice versa, while IRAK2 is present in both. The inference of mutual exclusivity (C76) is reasonable given the data, though temporal dynamics or sequential binding cannot be ruled out.

results.result: LPS stimulation induces binding of IRAK2 and ALYREF to Cxcl1, Cxcl2, and Tnf mRNAs, with ALYREF binding substantially reduced in IRAK2-deficient and kinase-inactive macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by RNA immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4C-D) showing LPS-induced binding and IRAK2-dependence. The data clearly demonstrate that ALYREF recruitment to target mRNAs requires IRAK2.

results.result: ALYREF-bound Cxcl1 and Tnf transcripts are increased in SRSF1 knockdown cells even in IRAK2 KO macrophages, indicating ALYREF binding is no longer IRAK2-dependent without SRSF1, suggesting IRAK2's role is to remove SRSF1 from target mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80, C82 are supported by RNA immunoprecipitation in SRSF1 knockdown cells (Figure 4E, G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This is a key experiment demonstrating that SRSF1 removal is the critical IRAK2-dependent step for ALYREF binding. The inference about IRAK2's role (C82) is well-supported.

results.result: ALYREF-bound Ctnnb1 mRNA is not affected by LPS stimulation, IRAK2 deficiency, or SRSF1 knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation (Figure 4E) showing no change in ALYREF binding to Ctnnb1 under various conditions. This negative control demonstrates specificity of the IRAK2-SRSF1-ALYREF pathway for specific mRNA targets.

results.result: Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNAs are efficiently exported to the cytosol in SRSF1 knockdown cells even in the absence of IRAK2.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by RT-PCR analysis of nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions (Figure 4F-G) showing cytosolic localization of target mRNAs in SRSF1 knockdown cells without IRAK2. This provides functional evidence that SRSF1 removal is sufficient for export, consistent with the proposed mechanism.

results.result: LPS induces IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction that requires ALYREF, suggesting IRAK2-ALYREF interaction is required for assembly of nuclear export complex including Nxf1 recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation showing LPS-induced IRAK2-Nxf1 interaction that is lost in ALYREF knockdown cells (Figure 5A). The inference about ALYREF's role in export complex assembly (C86) is reasonable given the known function of ALYREF as a bridge to Nxf1.

results.result: LPS stimulation induces Nxf1 binding to Cxcl1 and Tnf mRNAs in an ALYREF- and IRAK2-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5B-D) showing LPS-induced Nxf1 binding that is reduced in ALYREF knockdown and IRAK2 KO cells. This demonstrates the functional consequence of IRAK2-ALYREF interaction for export receptor recruitment.

results.result: LPS-induced Cxcl1, Cxcl2, and Tnf mRNAs accumulate in the nucleus in ALYREF knockdown cells, with dramatically reduced cytokine secretion, indicating ALYREF is important for IRAK2-mediated nuclear export of inflammatory mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by RT-PCR showing nuclear accumulation (Figure 5E) and ELISA showing reduced cytokine secretion (Figure 5F) in ALYREF knockdown cells. These data provide strong functional evidence for ALYREF's essential role in the export pathway.

results.result: SRSF1 binds to Cxcl1 3'UTR (nt 781-901), with nucleotides 800-855 being important for SRSF1 binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by REMSA experiments (Figure 6A) showing SRSF1 binding to Cxcl1 3'UTR and deletion analysis identifying the critical region. This provides direct biochemical evidence for SRSF1-mRNA interaction.

results.result: SRSF1 binds to luciferase reporter mRNA containing Cxcl1 3'UTR (nt 721-940), IRAK2 expression reduces this binding, and SRSF1 fails to bind mutated constructs lacking the SRSF1-binding region.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by RNA immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 6B) showing SRSF1 binding to wild-type but not mutant constructs, and reduced binding with IRAK2 expression. This provides functional validation of the SRSF1-binding site and IRAK2's effect on SRSF1-mRNA interaction.

results.result: IRAK2 strongly promotes luciferase activity and cytosolic localization of reporter mRNAs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR but has reduced ability with mutant constructs lacking SRSF1-binding sites, which are trapped in the nucleus, indicating SRSF1-binding sequence is required for IRAK2-promoted nuclear export.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 are supported by luciferase assays (Figure 6C) and RT-PCR of nuclear/cytoplasmic fractions (Figure 6D) showing IRAK2-dependent effects on wild-type but not mutant constructs. This is a critical experiment demonstrating that SRSF1-binding sites are necessary for IRAK2-mediated export, supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: LPS stimulation induces luciferase activity from constructs with wild-type Cxcl1 3'UTR (abolished in IRAK2-deficient cells), but activity is substantially reduced with mutant constructs in all cell types, confirming IRAK2-mediated nuclear export depends on SRSF1-binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by luciferase assays in macrophages (Figure 6E) showing LPS-induced, IRAK2-dependent activity with wild-type but not mutant constructs. This validates the findings in a more physiological context and confirms the mechanism.

results.result: IRAK2 promotes ALYREF binding to wild-type luciferase reporter mRNAs containing Cxcl1 3'UTR, but ALYREF shows reduced binding to mutant constructs even with IRAK2, suggesting SRSF1-binding site is required for ALYREF binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by RNA immunoprecipitation (Figure 6F) showing IRAK2-dependent ALYREF binding to wild-type but reduced binding to mutant constructs. The inference that SRSF1-binding sites are required for ALYREF binding (C108) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: ALYREF can directly bind to the probe containing the SRSF1-binding site (Cxcl1 nt 800-855) in vitro, indicating the SRSF1-binding site renders LPS-IRAK2 sensitivity for nuclear export via IRAK2-mediated SRSF1 removal and ALYREF recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is supported by REMSA (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing direct ALYREF binding to the SRSF1-binding site. Claim C110 is a reasonable synthesis of all the luciferase and binding data, though the mechanism remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: IRAK2 kinase-inactive knockin mice show substantially increased survival after LPS-induced septic shock and much reduced serum CXCL1 and TNF levels compared to wild-type mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by survival curves (Figure 7A) and ELISA of serum cytokines (Figure 7B). These in vivo data provide important validation that the IRAK2 kinase activity requirement observed in vitro has physiological relevance for inflammatory responses and disease outcomes.

results.result: LPS/TLR4 engagement activates a nuclear function of IRAK2 where kinase activity enables RanBP2-mediated sumoylation and nuclear translocation, nuclear IRAK2 phosphorylates SRSF1 to reduce its binding to target mRNAs, LPS induces IRAK2-ALYREF interaction to replace SRSF1, and recruited ALYREF bridges mRNA-Nxf1 interaction for export, providing a critical checkpoint for inflammatory cytokine production.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. These are well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence including biochemical interactions, functional assays, mutant analysis, and in vivo validation. The proposed mechanism is internally consistent and supported by the data, though some steps remain somewhat inferential.

results.result: RanBP2 is a major nucleoporin with phenylalanine-glycine repeats that bind importin beta family receptors, and phosphorylation of IRAK2 at S136/T140 affects its interaction with RanBP2.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is supported by prior literature (Wu et al., 1995; Yokoyama et al., 1995). Claim C123 is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with phosphorylation site mutants. These provide important mechanistic details about the IRAK2-RanBP2 interaction.

results.result: ALYREF and SRSF1 belong to the same family of shuttling SR proteins sharing similar RNA-binding domains, both can bind the same SRSF1-binding motif, and SRSF1 removal allows ALYREF binding, suggesting SRSF1-mediated nuclear sequestration is achieved by blocking ALYREF binding.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is established knowledge. Claims C125-C127 are supported by REMSA showing both proteins bind the same motif and RNA immunoprecipitation in SRSF1 knockdown cells. The inference about the mechanism of SRSF1-mediated sequestration (C127) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: ALYREF (TREX complex subunit) makes contact with nuclear export receptor Nxf1 serving as a bridge between mRNA and Nxf1, and nuclear IRAK2 mediates SRSF1 removal and facilitates assembly of nuclear export machinery for inflammatory mRNA export.
results.evaluation: Claim C128 is supported by prior literature on ALYREF function. Claim C129 is a summary conclusion well-supported by the experimental data. These provide important context and synthesis of the findings.

results.result: About 10-30% of LPS-induced inflammatory transcripts are exported in the absence of IRAK2, suggesting there might be another mechanism besides IRAK2 that allows ALYREF binding to target mRNAs for nuclear export.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is supported by RT-PCR data (Figure 3B) showing partial export without IRAK2. Claim C131 is speculative, acknowledging incomplete understanding of the export mechanisms. While the observation is valid, the alternative mechanism is not characterized, making this an area for future investigation rather than a supported conclusion.
